connection: The production repository and services are still synchronous because their List-based work performs no external I/O. Session 26 introduces Task, Task<T>, async, and await honestly in the permanent ScratchPad notebook.
objectives: Explain that Task represents eventual completion and Task<T> represents eventual completion plus a value of type T.
Explain that Task and the async keyword do not automatically create a background thread.
Use await to obtain the string carried by Task<string> while preserving readable control flow.
Use Task.FromResult and Task.CompletedTask as already-completed Task examples without calling them genuine asynchronous work.

visuals.title: Task is a handle to eventual completion
visuals.explanation: A Task records whether an operation is incomplete, completed, faulted, or cancelled. It does not by itself say which thread performed the work.

visuals.title: Task<T> carries a result
visuals.explanation: Task<string> represents completion plus a string. await nameTask waits for completion when necessary and gives the method the string result.

visuals.title: Already-completed work still fits the Task shape
visuals.explanation: Task.FromResult("Parm") returns a Task<string> that is already complete because Parm is already known. It creates no I/O and no background thread.

visuals.title: Async flows to the caller
visuals.explanation: RunAsync awaits a Task, so it returns Task. ScratchPad's top-level Program.cs directly awaits RunAsync before continuing.

preQuiz.prompt: What extra information does Task<string> represent compared with Task?
options: A string that is already printed
preQuiz.explanation: Task represents completion; Task<string> represents completion plus a string value.

preQuiz.prompt: Does marking a method async automatically create a new thread?
options: Only when the method returns Task<string>
preQuiz.explanation: async enables await and shapes Task-returning control flow; it does not promise another thread.
The string is already known, so Task.FromResult wraps it in an already-completed Task<string>.

concept.title: Task and Task<T> describe completion
paragraphs: Task is a handle to an operation's eventual completion. Task<T> adds a result of type T. For Task<string>, the eventual result is a string.

Neither Task nor async automatically creates a background thread. An operation may complete synchronously, wait for genuine I/O, or be completed by another mechanism. The Task shape alone does not decide that.

rows: Eventual completion without a returned value
An already-completed Task without a result
Waits when necessary and gives back the string

concept.title: await unwraps the result
paragraphs: GetEmployeeNameAsync returns Task<string>. RunAsync first stores that Task without awaiting it, making the Task itself observable. await nameTask then produces the string carried by the Task.
RunAsync is declared async Task because it uses await but returns no value to its caller. An async Task method normally reaches the end of its body; it does not explicitly return Task.CompletedTask.
concept.code:
Task<string> nameTask = GetEmployeeNameAsync();
string employeeName = await nameTask;

concept.title: Already-completed work is an experiment, not production I/O
paragraphs: The value Parm is already available. Task.FromResult wraps it in a completed Task<string> so the learner can practice Task and await. It does not make the lookup asynchronous.

The production repository remains synchronous because List.Add, Where, and FirstOrDefault execute in memory. Real asynchronous repository work belongs later, when EF Core or another external I/O boundary provides operations worth awaiting.

concept.title: Optional sidebar — Reading IntelliSense signatures
paragraphs: IntelliSense may show Task<TResult>(Func<TResult> function). For Task<string>, TResult becomes string. Func<string> means callable code that returns a string, and () => "Parm" is one such callable value.

new Task<string>(() => "Parm") creates an unstarted Task that would require Start. That legal API does not express this experiment's intent. Task.FromResult("Parm") directly creates the already-completed Task<string> needed here.
IntelliSense shows legal API choices; it does not decide which choice best communicates the program's intent.

lab.title: Observe a Task Before and After await
lab.objective: Build a permanent ScratchPad experiment that observes Task<string>, awaits its already-completed value, and prints the value without pretending the operation performs real I/O.
lab.task: Create AsyncFlowExperiments, observe the Task returned by a helper, await its string result, and invoke RunAsync from ScratchPad Program.cs.
lab.startingCondition: Session 25's ResourceExperiments remains in src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.ScratchPad. Production repositories and services remain synchronous and unchanged.

steps.text: In project src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.ScratchPad, create folder Session26 and file src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.ScratchPad/Session26/AsyncFlowExperiments.cs. Setup code: add a comment identifying this as the Session 26 Task and await experiment.

In project src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.ScratchPad, folder Session26, file AsyncFlowExperiments.cs, declare public sealed class AsyncFlowExperiments. Remember: sealed says this focused experiment class is not intended as a base class.

In project src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.ScratchPad, folder Session26, file AsyncFlowExperiments.cs, inside AsyncFlowExperiments, add public Task RunAsync() with a temporary body that throws NotImplementedException. Setup code: paste the temporary throw; the Async suffix signals a Task-returning method.

In project src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.ScratchPad, folder Session26, file AsyncFlowExperiments.cs, inside AsyncFlowExperiments but outside RunAsync, add private Task<string> GetEmployeeNameAsync() with a temporary throw. Remember: Task<string> means eventual completion plus a string.

In project src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.ScratchPad, folder Session26, file AsyncFlowExperiments.cs, inside GetEmployeeNameAsync, replace the temporary throw with return Task.FromResult("Parm");. Learning code: write this line yourself. Parm is already known, so this creates an already-completed Task<string>, not real asynchronous work.
From the csharp-practice-working solution folder, build project src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.ScratchPad as a safe checkpoint before implementing RunAsync.

In project src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.ScratchPad, folder Session26, file AsyncFlowExperiments.cs, inside RunAsync, replace the temporary throw by calling GetEmployeeNameAsync without await and storing the result in Task<string> nameTask. Then print Before await: followed by nameTask.GetType().Name. Learning code: write these statements yourself.

In project src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.ScratchPad, folder Session26, file AsyncFlowExperiments.cs, change RunAsync from public Task to public async Task. Still inside RunAsync, await nameTask and store the unwrapped result in string employeeName. Remember: async does not create a thread; await obtains the Task<string> result.

In project src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.ScratchPad, folder Session26, file AsyncFlowExperiments.cs, at the end of RunAsync, print After await: followed by employeeName. An async Task method normally ends here without explicitly returning a Task.

In project src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.ScratchPad, file src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.ScratchPad/Program.cs, in the top-level statements after the earlier session calls, instantiate AsyncFlowExperiments in asyncFlowExperiments and await asyncFlowExperiments.RunAsync(). Top-level Program.cs can use await directly.

From the csharp-practice-working solution folder, run project src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.ScratchPad. Observe the Task type before await and Parm after await. Explain aloud why Task.FromResult did not create real asynchronous work.
From the csharp-practice-working solution folder, build PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln in Release and run the complete test suite without rebuilding. Open Solution Reveal only after both commands pass.
steps.code:
dotnet build PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln --configuration Release
dotnet test PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln --configuration Release --no-build

reveals.title: Solution
reveals.text: The helper returns an already-completed Task<string>. RunAsync observes the Task, awaits its string result, and Program awaits RunAsync.

lab.expectedBehavior:
Before await: Task`1
After await: Parm

The exact runtime Task type name may include implementation detail, but the first line observes a Task<string> and the second line observes the string obtained by await.

commit: session-26: teach tasks and awaitable work
review: Production interfaces, repositories, services, App behavior, and tests remain unchanged.
Every created Task is deliberately awaited or returned; no async void, Task.Run, CancellationToken, or fire-and-forget call was added.
Setup code is distinguished from learning code, reminders reinforce meaning without padding, and all steps use Step n/n.
The complete implementation remains hidden behind the existing Solution Reveal.

postQuiz.prompt: After string employeeName = await nameTask;, what is employeeName?
postQuiz.explanation: await unwraps the completed Task<string> result.

postQuiz.prompt: Why does GetEmployeeNameAsync use Task.FromResult in this lesson?
options: To practice the Task<T> contract with an already-known value
To force work onto a background thread
postQuiz.explanation: Task.FromResult is an honest already-completed adapter for the experiment, not genuine asynchronous work.

postQuiz.prompt: Why does RunAsync end without return Task.CompletedTask;?
options: The compiler completes the returned Task when an async Task method reaches the end
postQuiz.explanation: An async Task method normally reaches the end of its body; the compiler manages its returned Task.

reflections: What is observable before await, and what value becomes available after await?
Why would new Task<string>(() => "Parm") communicate the wrong intent for this experiment?
What future repository change would introduce genuine I/O worth awaiting?
whatBreaks: Removing await from nameTask leaves a Task<string> rather than the employee name. Removing await from the top-level RunAsync call allows Program.cs to continue without deliberately observing completion. Replacing Task.FromResult with new Task<string>(...) creates an unstarted Task and causes await to wait forever unless separate code starts it.
summary: Task represents eventual completion; Task<T> also carries a result. async does not create a thread, await obtains a Task<T> result, and Task.FromResult creates an already-completed Task<T> for this isolated experiment. Production stays synchronous until a genuine I/O boundary exists.
